summary:
We developed **Crew Health Companion**, a prototype web application that helps astronauts keep track of their health and daily routines during space missions.

The application brings health information together in one place. Astronauts can record health measurements, describe symptoms, track sleep and alertness, view trends, and maintain a history of health-related events. It also includes a diet plan and daily schedule. If an astronaut misses a meal, the application can suggest a free time slot to eat later. A medical support summary helps them share relevant information with their crew medical team.

Our project addresses the challenge of managing health alongside a demanding mission schedule, especially when astronauts are far from immediate medical support. By making information easier to record and review, it aims to help astronauts recognise concerns, follow up on them, and maintain their routines.

This is important for longer missions, where crew wellbeing and the ability to manage health information are essential. The prototype provides guidance, not a medical diagnosis.
details:
Crew Health Companion

Crew Health Companion is a prototype web application designed to help astronauts organise their health information and manage daily routines during space missions. It brings health tracking, symptom reporting, meal scheduling and reference information together in one place.

What does it do, and how does it work?

The dashboard gives astronauts an overview of their recorded information and highlights items that may need attention.

In the vitals section, astronauts can manually enter measurements such as blood pressure, blood sugar and bone density. The app displays their status against example ranges. These ranges are placeholders and would need to be set and reviewed by a mission medical team.

The symptom check and journal allow astronauts to describe how they feel in their own words and record details such as what has changed, any measurements, and whether a concern affects their work. They can also add follow-up information about whether a concern has improved, stayed the same or worsened.

The trends section lets astronauts record sleep and alertness and compare their entries over time. It also includes a mood and stress check-in. A separate history section allows them to add, view, edit and import past health records.

The diet plan works alongside a daily schedule. Astronauts can record whether they ate or missed a meal. When a meal is missed, the application can suggest a free time slot; the astronaut can review and accept the suggestion.

The app can prepare a medical handoff summary of recorded readings and concerns for the astronaut to share through their mission’s medical communication channel. It also includes an offline reference guide and a backup and restore option.

Benefits and intended impact

Astronauts have demanding schedules and may experience health changes during a mission. Our project aims to make it easier to keep relevant information organised, notice patterns, follow up on concerns and communicate clearly with medical professionals.

By connecting meal tracking with the daily schedule, it also aims to help astronauts make time for nutrition. We hope the project can contribute to crew wellbeing and help astronauts manage their routines during longer missions.

Tools, languages and software

We developed the prototype as a web application using HTML, CSS and JavaScript. It runs in a web browser and stores entries locally in that browser, allowing its current features to be used offline.

The prototype does not currently connect to medical sensors, send messages or automatically share data with ground crew. It provides guidance rather than a medical diagnosis.

What makes the project creative?

Our approach brings health tracking and daily scheduling together. For example, the app does more than record a missed meal: it looks for an available time in the schedule and offers a possible alternative. It also combines symptom notes, past history and health readings into a handoff summary to support communication with the medical team.

Factors we considered

We considered astronauts’ workloads, nutrition, sleep, physical and mental wellbeing, access to previous records, limited connectivity and the need for medical guidance. We also considered what might happen if an astronaut is unable to manually report a concern.

Future development

Following feedback from the local judging round, we would like to explore connecting the application to approved health-monitoring devices and enabling automatic updates to an authorised ground medical team when communication is available. A future system could flag concerning readings or missed check-ins, reducing reliance on the astronaut manually sending a message.

If communication is unavailable, a future version could store updates onboard and send them when the connection returns. These capabilities would require suitable hardware, secure communication, medical review and testing.
